We thank the reviewer for the comment. Due to the limited time during the rebuttal discussion phase, we were unable to evaluate the suggested min(max(p(a|s)))) baseline, but we'll include it in the final revision. To provide additional insight in the interim, we previously experimented with a baseline using training loss as a branching metric, where the branching points are selected from positions with policy loss exceeding a tunable threshold. While not identical, this approach shares a conceptual similarity to the reviewer's suggestion, as the policy loss reflects policy uncertainty. In our experiments, this baseline performed only slightly better than random branching and consistently underperformed the baseline without branching and our method. We observed that training loss is often sensitive to rarely visited or unseen states. This suggests that simple uncertainty proxies may often require additional heuristics or regularization to be effective in practice. On the other hand, our LCR method can be interpreted as a generalization of selecting nodes in a value range (such as 0.3~0.7), and our work provides insights into the interpretability of varying LCR threshold corresponding to varying the value range.

We'll provide more simulation results for the RMSE analysis in the final revision due to limited compute resources during the rebuttal discussion phase. We again thank the reviewer for the feedback.

Thank you for your detailed responses and additional experiments. My primary concern remains that the chosen baseline (random branching) is too weak. The key contribution of your work should be focused on effectively selecting intermediate positions from which exploration yields valuable information to update the model. Simple alternatives such as MCTS value-based or policy uncertainty-based methods (e.g., for value between 0.3~0.7, select the node with min(max(p(a|s)))) should perform better than random and serve as stronger baselines. Therefore, my primary interest is in confirming experimentally whether your proposed method demonstrates clear advantages over these simpler approaches.

To clarify, my suggestion is not yet as demanding as methods in the "Learning to Stop" paper, where an uncertainty network needs to be trained. Nor do I currently ask you to consider shifts in value or policy during prolonged MCTS searches. Rather, my goal is to see clear evidence that your method surpasses simpler and intuitive baselines.

Additionally, I appreciate the provided RMSE analyses for various simulation counts. Could you include more extensive results, such as simulations counts of 5, 10, 25, 50, and possibly 1600, to further confirm robustness across a wider range of scenarios?

We thank the reviewer for the feedback. We have conducted additional experiments for the rebuttal, and we will include them in the final revision, as this year's rebuttal phase doesn't allow authors to upload a PDF or any images. We address each comment as follows:

**Q**: Generalization to the non-Bernoulli case: In the Discussion section, you allude to the possibility of using quantiles. Is there any obstruction to obtaining a similar closed form for common distributions, like Gaussian or Beta distributions?

**A**: The generalization to the non-Bernoulli case typically does not yield a closed form when computing Pr(|X-Y| > t), as the sum (or difference) of two independent random variables is the convolution of their distributions. However, in practice, the integration can be estimated using numerical techniques.

**Q**: Is it possible to add uncertainty bands / error bars to some figures (such as Figures 6b, 7b, 8a, and 8b)? I assume that these can be obtained by running multiple trials and using a metric such as standard error, or a confidence interval.

**A**: We'll include the standard deviation and confidence interval in the revision. The standard deviation for Figure 6 (b) and Figure 7(b) is about 1.0% and Figure 8 is about 2.1%.

**Q**: Can this approach be extended to n-player games, as in Multiplayer AlphaZero?

**A**: We believe our approach can be extended to n-player settings. Since our method leverages the MCTS value and LCR estimation to quantify uncertainty, it is, in general, compatible with Multiplayer AlphaZero and similar variants.

> Page-by-page comments and suggestions:

We will incorporate the comments and suggestions into the final revision. We provide clarifications as follows:

> Page 2:
> "change decisions after the tree search"

This refers to the difference between the best action decided by the NN policy and the one selected after performing MCTS. This concept is further discussed in Section 2.2.

> Page 6:
> "fluctuate around"

This describes situations where win rate values remain close to the initial value across time steps. For example: …, 0.6, 0.62, 0.58, 0.59, … indicates fluctuation around 0.6.

> "capture the turning point"

This refers to identifying positions where a significant change in win rate occurs, such as a sudden drop from 0.59 to 0.1, which might reflect a critical mistake or forced move. The LCR can be used to detect such turning points.

> Page 9:
> "our method achieves equivalent strength"

This refers to achieving the same playing strength when comparing ours to the baseline.

We again thank the reviewer for their feedback to improve the clarity of our work.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback. We have conducted additional experiments for the rebuttal, and we will include them in the final revision, as this year's rebuttal phase doesn't allow authors to upload a PDF or any images. We address each comment as follows:

> Using random selection as the baseline for branching is weak, as obviously certain positions should not be explored from.

Our method is designed to achieve two complementary goals: (1) reducing variance through value ensembling from multiple games, and (2) exploring overlooked but potentially promising decisions. The random branching baseline highlights the limitations of relying solely on (1) and demonstrates the importance of branching position selection in our proposed strategy.

> There is no direct comparison with the MCTS value baseline. Theoretically, MCTS values themselves inherently capture uncertainty effectively.

We agree that MCTS value inherently captures uncertainty. Typically, there are two ways to model this uncertainty: the frequentist and the Bayesian perspectives. Our method adopts a Bayesian interpretation, where the MCTS value is assumed to be a random variable, rather than a fixed estimate. This choice does not imply that the Bayesian approach is universally better for modeling uncertainty in MCTS values; instead, it reflects the specific interests of our setting. In particular, our proposed branching method typically only has a small number of variations (V), placing us in a low-sample regime. As a result, Bayesian methods can offer more sample efficiency than frequentist ones by incorporating the assumed prior distribution and explicitly modeling uncertainty, as analyzed in Section 4.1 for the Bernoulli distribution. We thank the reviewer for raising this point, and we will include a discussion in the revision.

> The authors only consider uncertainty in terms of value estimation but neglect uncertainty related to policy decisions. For instance, methods such as those described in the "Learning to Stop" paper might be more appropriate, especially since agents can directly simulate outcomes. Furthermore, many states, such as the initial state, can remain persistently uncertain in value, regardless of the number of simulations performed.

Our method focuses on identifying high-uncertainty positions that can alter the game result, as value labels exhibit high variance in the original AlphaZero self-play process. In particular, for positions with low value uncertainty but high policy uncertainty, even though there is significant variability in the move to play (high policy uncertainty), the game result is also highly determined (low value uncertainty). In general, in addition to exploring the uncertainty position, our work also aims to reduce the value label variance. Exploring positions with low value uncertainty but with high policy uncertainty is left as future work.

> The authors do not explore alternative uncertainty estimation methods sufficiently. For example, if MCTS value remains stable throughout the search of a state, it may indicate inherent certainty in the uncertainty itself rather than genuine uncertainty about the position. Conversely, fluctuating values might signify genuine uncertainty and an area needing further training.

In addition to the previous discussion, our work focuses on analyzing the proposed LCR metric, and we include a discussion of alternative uncertainty estimation in Appendix A.2.4. We appreciate the reviewer's perspective, and future studies on incorporating uncertainty during search can complement our work.

> The chosen threshold (lcr_0=0.48) appears arbitrary. A more principled approach, such as selecting the top 10% most uncertain positions, might yield better performance.

The choice of LCR_0 is based on the initial value (0.6) for an empty position. The threshold serves as an interpretable hyperparameter and can be adjusted accordingly with different value thresholds. On the other hand, we adopt a fixed threshold to ensure that branching occurs only at positions with sufficiently high variability. This is particularly important in cases where none of the positions in a game are suitable for branching due to the exploration noise introduced in the self-play. For instance, as discussed in the visualization in Appendix A.1, some games have few to no branching points (shown in entirely blue lines) due to exploring a clearly losing position. In such cases, enforcing a fixed-percentage strategy could lead to branching at low-variability positions, potentially reducing the overall quality of exploration. Conversely, there are games where more than 30% of the positions exhibit high LCR. Overall, we find that using a fixed threshold offers a flexible way to ensure efficient exploration across diverse game scenarios.

> Additionally, the optimal number of variations (V=10) was determined empirically without providing deeper insights or theoretical justifications for why this specific number is particularly effective.

Our observations show that increasing V allows for a broader exploration of uncertainty at the selected positions and leads to improved performance. Understanding this distribution could offer insights into which game phases most benefit from the proposed branching strategy.

To summarize the figure, the data distribution shows a higher density of uncertain positions in the early stages of the game. Since our branching strategy aims to capture the turning point in the later game phase, the figure shows the sample distribution peak around move 110. We appreciate the reviewer's suggestion, as it helped us better illustrate how our proposed LCR metric quantifies uncertainty across various phases of the game.

Our proposed method preserves the training targets unbiased, as in standard AlphaZero: policy labels come from the MCTS visit counts, and value labels remain the unbiased average of game returns. Moreover, the AlphaZero algorithm doesn't promise global optimality but instead relies on iterative policy improvement via self‑play MCTS [1]. Because our method does not modify the PUCT formula and the MCTS policy‑improvement operator, each iteration under the shifted visit distribution remains a valid policy‑improvement step, although the sequence of improved policies may differ from the original AlphaZero. As a result, we still retain AlphaZero's core policy improvement behavior. Overall, we acknowledge that a quantitative analysis on the final policy optimality of the AlphaZero algorithm and its variants remains an open problem for future investigation.

**A**: In the revised version, we'll include a graph showing the distribution for positions whose LCR exceeds a LCR threshold. More specifically, the graph will show a gradual increase in percentage for each move as the LCR threshold is decreased. At LCR_0 = 0.47, 3 positions are included.

At LCR_0 = 0.46, 4 positions are included.

The paper tackles a long-standing inefficiency in AlphaZero-style self-play: most positions are visited only once and the single game result used as a training target is noisy.

The authors propose **Uncertainty-Guided Branching (UGB)**:

- Label Change Rate – an analytic, closed-form estimate of how likely the game outcome would flip if the same position were replayed. A Bayesian update refines LCR when repeated roll-outs are available.
- Where / how / what to branch – positions whose posterior LCR exceeds a threshold are selected; 10 runner-up MCTS moves are replayed from each such position; their outcomes are ensembled to reduce value-label variance.
- Extensive experiments on 9 × 9 and 19 × 19 Go shows an improved sample efficiency over the baseline by 58.5% on 9x9 Go in the early stage of training and by 47.3% on 19x19 Go in the late stage of training.

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel uncertainty-guided exploration of positions in self-play for AlphaZero. Using a proposed Label Change Rate (LCR) metric, positions with high uncertainty are identified after self-play trajectories are generated.  The LCR values are used to sample an uncertain state, and a new action is sampled from the policy in that state, generating a new trajectory. This is repeated V times, and all the generated trajectories are used to estimate values of states and as training data for the Neural Network training phase of AlphaZero. Experimental results show the accuracy of the LCR metric, and the sample efficiency gains of the proposed method, in two variants of Go.

summary.value:
This paper addresses an important and practical problem: enhancing exploration efficiency in AlphaZero's training process. The authors correctly point out the inefficiency inherent in AlphaZero’s traditional approach of initiating self-play games from the starting position every time, leaving many high-uncertainty states under-explored.

To resolve this issue, the authors introduce a well-defined uncertainty estimation metric called "Label Change Rate (LCR)." LCR intuitively and effectively quantifies state uncertainty by calculating the variability of outcomes from the same position across multiple game plays. The authors further solidify this approach through a robust Bayesian inference framework. This method clearly identifies the core of the problem and serves as a strong baseline.

The experimental design is thorough: initially validating the effectiveness and accuracy of LCR, then analyzing the impact of different branching strategies and positions on exploration efficiency, and finally demonstrating the benefits through comprehensive end-to-end training evaluations. Overall, the experimental results are convincing, showing that the proposed uncertainty-guided exploration method significantly improves AlphaZero’s training efficiency and performance.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
Mentioned in the summary. 

Weakness:
- Using random selection as the baseline for branching is weak, as obviously certain positions should not be explored from.

- There is no direct comparison with the MCTS value baseline. Theoretically, MCTS values themselves inherently capture uncertainty effectively.

- The authors only consider uncertainty in terms of value estimation but neglect uncertainty related to policy decisions. For instance, methods such as those described in the "Learning to Stop" paper might be more appropriate, especially since agents can directly simulate outcomes. Furthermore, many states, such as the initial state, can remain persistently uncertain in value, regardless of the number of simulations performed.

- The authors do not explore alternative uncertainty estimation methods sufficiently. For example, if MCTS value remains stable throughout the search of a state, it may indicate inherent certainty in the uncertainty itself rather than genuine uncertainty about the position. Conversely, fluctuating values might signify genuine uncertainty and an area needing further training.

- The chosen threshold (lcr_0=0.48) appears arbitrary. A more principled approach, such as selecting the top 10% most uncertain positions, might yield better performance. Additionally, the optimal number of variations (V=10) was determined empirically without providing deeper insights or theoretical justifications for why this specific number is particularly effective.

questions.value:
Distribution of LCR-Uncertain States:
Could the authors provide an analysis of how the LCR-uncertain states are distributed across different game stages (e.g., early, mid, late game)? Understanding this distribution could offer insights into which game phases most benefit from the proposed branching strategy.

Impact of MCTS Simulation Counts on LCR Accuracy:
It would be valuable to investigate how the accuracy of the LCR metric varies with different MCTS simulation counts. Considering recent methods frequently utilize fewer simulations (e.g., 100-200), compared to traditional settings (e.g., 800), evaluating LCR across varying simulation counts could validate its robustness and practical applicability.

Clarification on RMSE Analysis Methodology:
The current RMSE evaluation approach is not entirely clear. A suitable method might involve first obtaining multiple simulation results (like geting n=1000 z values) for each of the 20,000 positions, calculating their average as the ground truth, and then comparing this ground truth with estimates obtained from varying numbers of simulations (from 1 up to V=10). Could the authors clarify or consider revising their RMSE analysis accordingly?

summary.value: The authors propose an uncertainty-guided MCTS exploration framework that improves upon standard AlphaZero. It branches out from high-uncertainty positions and explores multiple variations. This reduces the variance of the value label by ensembling multiple game outcomes. It also explores critical decision points that may yield improvements. This results in greater training efficiency.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The experimental results look promising. I suggest adding error bars to some of the Figures (such as 6b, 7b, 8a, and 8b). These can be obtained by running multiple trials. Overall, the idea of uncertainty-guided exploration during MCTS makes a lot of sense.

Page-by-page comments and suggestions:

Page 1:

"It learns through self-play" No need for italics and boldface here.

"alternative fashion" → "alternating fashion"

"the strength" → "the agent's playing strength"

Page 2:

"change decisions after the tree search" Unclear what this means. Change from the policy head's prediction? If so, state so.

"during self-play while" Add comma before while.

Reduce the indentation of the contribution list.

"our analysis on Bernoulli distribution" → "our analysis of/on the Bernoulli distribution"

"in an analytical form" → "in an analytical way" / "via an analytical form" ?

Page 3:

"policy and value to obtain the search result, typically requiring hundreds to thousands
of neural network predictions to obtain a search result." Repetition of "to obtain a/the search result".

"red arrow in the figure" → "red arrow in Figure 2"

Page 4:

"In this section, we... in Section 4.1" Redundant to say "in section X" twice.

"denoted by θ = LCR(s)" Put LCR in upright font for consistency.

Lines 141-143 are a run-on sentence. Split into at least two sentences.

Page 5:

Algorithm 1: "has been played" should not be italicized.

Algorithm 1: "play_episode_from" consider using normal text and font (as opposed to monospace with underscores) for consistency with the rest of the presentation of the algorithm.

"and thus can reduce the label variance" doesn't grammatically fit with the rest of the sentence. Consider making it a new sentence: "This reduces the label variance".

Page 6:

"where LCR0 represents" Put LCR in upright font for consistency.

"so that we can discard positions whose win rates fluctuate around the initial win rate" Unclear what this means. What precisely do you mean by "fluctuate around"? Consider rephrasing or elaborating.

"positions are weighted by their time step because we want to capture the turning point in the later game phase" Unclear what "capture the turning point" means here. Consider clarifying.

"when G number of states are collected, and this hyperparameter is the same as..." → "when G states are collected, where G is the same hyperparameter as..."

"In this section, ... in Section 5.1" Redundant.

"Each training" → "Each training run"

Page 7:

"analytical estimators with" Add comma before "with".

Page 8:

"similar to our method" → "similarly to our method"

Page 9:

"our method achieves equivalent strength" Equivalent to what? Standard AlphaZero? Clarify.

"allow the return to a specific state" → "allows the algorithm to return to a specific state", if that's what you meant.

title.value: Uncertainty-Guided Exploration for Efficient AlphaZero Training

abstract.value: AlphaZero has achieved remarkable success in complex decision-making problems through self-play and neural network training. However, its self-play process remains inefficient due to limited exploration of high-uncertainty positions, the overlooked runner-up decisions in Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), and high variance in value labels. To address these challenges, we propose and evaluate uncertainty-guided exploration by branching from high-uncertainty positions using our proposed Label Change Rate (LCR) metric, which is further refined by a Bayesian inference framework. Our proposed approach leverages runner-up MCTS decisions to create multiple variations, and ensembles value labels across these variations to reduce variance. We investigate three key design parameters for our branching strategy: where to branch, how many variations to branch, and which move to play in the new branch. Our empirical findings indicate that branching with 10 variations per game provides the best performance-exploration balance. Overall, our end-to-end results show an improved sample efficiency over the baseline by 58.5\% on 9x9 Go in the early stage of training and by 47.3\% on 19x19 Go in the late stage of training.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and ensure all material is anonymized. The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22)

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.

The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
